candidates.title: People remember famous logos confidently, consistently and wrongly (visual Mandela effect)
candidates.claim: Feature on the Brain Bridge Lab (Univ. of Chicago) study: Apple and Ralph Lauren logos picked correctly by ~80%; Monopoly man, Volkswagen and Fruit of the Loom by only 20-30%; people repeat the same errors when drawing from memory.
candidates.verification: Primary study verified: Prasad & Bainbridge (2022) Psychological Science 33(12):1971-1988 (APS Observer, 2024); UChicago News 2022-07-15. Cause not known; schema theory ruled out as universal explanation (Fruit of the Loom cornucopia chosen over the more 'fitting' plate).
candidates.note: News spark is a fresh feature (4 Nov 2026) on a peer-reviewed study. Strongest concrete image: a monocle that never existed.

candidates.title: 85 students tried to draw the Apple logo from memory; 1 succeeded
candidates.claim: Blake, Nazarian & Castel (2015), Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology: 1 of 85 drew it correctly; fewer than half picked the real logo among altered versions; striking gap between confidence and performance.
candidates.verification: University release + paper PDF on castel.psych.ucla.edu (not opened). Use only as support; Apple was yesterday's topic so keep it to one line or the caption.

lenses_summary.verification_red_team: C1 rests on a peer-reviewed paper (Prasad & Bainbridge 2022, Psychological Science 33(12)); the 4 Nov 2026 Creative Bloq piece is a fresh feature on it, not new research: never say 'new study'. Numbers to keep exact: ~80% correct for Apple and Ralph Lauren, 20-30% for Monopoly man, Volkswagen, Fruit of the Loom; 100 participants in study 1. The 'half drew a monocle' figure appears only in a secondary source (APS Observer) — avoid or say 'many'. The cause is NOT known; schema theory is NOT the full explanation (Fruit of the Loom counterexample). Do not claim 'the brain fills in what fits the story' as fact. C2 (1 of 85 drew Apple logo) verified via UCLA release; use sparingly (Apple was yesterday).
lenses_summary.audience_psychology: Huge 'wait, what?' moment: the viewer is sure Monopoly man has a monocle and is wrong. Self-test = saves, shares, comments. Ego-safe lesson for owners: you think customers know your logo; they hold a confident, shared, wrong version. Works identically for Persian and English audiences (global icons, Volkswagen and Fruit of the Loom known in both).
lenses_summary.brand_fit: Identity + consumer memory: core Behnood territory. Owner takeaway (café, bakery, salon, shop): ask five customers to draw your sign from memory; what survives is your real brand; design one detail worth remembering and accept that the rest blurs. Avoid drawing or generating any character (Monopoly man, Pikachu, Waldo, C-3PO) or logo: use generic objects (monocle, horn, fruit, pencil, eraser) and only owner-uploaded real images.

gates.brand_fit_gate: C1 passes; C4 fails (naming repeat of 10-31); C5, C6, C9 fail (overlap with 10-24/10-26); C7 fails (cause/sensitive, not brand strategy); C11 fails (unverifiable).
gates.story_gate: C1: tension = 'they're sure they know your brand; they remember a version you never made'; concrete image = a monocle on a table that never belonged to the man everyone pictures. Beats C3 (good tension, weaker single image, single source).
